difficultyReason: One-step conditional gap. Stimulus places Dr. Aronson in a named category; conclusion moves her to a second category; the correct answer supplies the missing universal link between the two categories.
stimulus: Every physician at Brighton Clinic is certified in emergency medicine. Dr. Aronson practices at Brighton Clinic. So Dr. Aronson is qualified to staff the county trauma ward.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone certified in emergency medicine is qualified to staff the county trauma ward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some physicians qualified to staff the county trauma ward are certified in emergency medicine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No physician who lacks certification in emergency medicine practices at Brighton Clinic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone qualified to staff the county trauma ward is certified in emergency medicine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most physicians at Brighton Clinic have staffed a trauma ward at some point in their careers.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that Dr. Aronson is certified in emergency medicine. To force the conclusion that she is qualified to staff the trauma ward, we need every emergency-certified physician to be so qualified. (A) supplies exactly that universal bridge.
explanations.B: Too weak. 'Some' qualified staffers being certified does not put Dr. Aronson in the qualified group.
explanations.C: This restates the first premise in contrapositive form. It tells us who can practice at Brighton, not who is trauma-ward qualified.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional. This says qualified → certified, but the argument needs certified → qualified.
explanations.E: 'Most' does not guarantee Dr. Aronson is among them, and past staffing is not the same as present qualification.

difficultyReason: Single-step gap between 'breaks a promise' and 'acts wrongly.' The correct answer is a universal ethical principle that closes the gap directly.
stimulus: Ethicist: Councilor Marsh pledged during her campaign to vote against the stadium subsidy, but last week she voted in favor of it. In doing so, she broke a promise she had made to her constituents. Therefore, Councilor Marsh acted wrongly.
questionStem: The ethicist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who breaks a promise made to constituents acts wrongly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A councilor who votes for a stadium subsidy acts wrongly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most promises made during political campaigns ought to be kept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone who acts wrongly has broken a promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No councilor who keeps her campaign promises acts wrongly.

explanations.correct: The premise establishes that Marsh broke a promise to her constituents. To force the conclusion that she acted wrongly, the argument needs the universal 'breaking such a promise → acting wrongly.' (A) is that conditional.
explanations.B: The stimulus never claims that voting for the subsidy is itself wrong — only that breaking the promise is the wrong act.
explanations.C: 'Most' is too weak to force a conclusion about Marsh's particular promise.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional: wrong → promise-breaking, rather than promise-breaking → wrong.
explanations.E: Tells us only what follows when promises are kept; Marsh did not keep hers, so this yields no conclusion about her conduct.

difficultyReason: Direct one-concept gap. Premise identifies a firm as a monopolist; conclusion attributes a consequence (raises prices above competitive levels). Correct answer is the universal linking the two.
stimulus: Economist: Northgate Utilities is the sole provider of natural gas in this region and therefore operates as a monopolist. It follows that Northgate charges prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.
questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every monopolist charges prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any firm that charges prices above competitive levels is a monopolist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monopolists tend to charge higher prices than firms facing competitors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A firm that is the sole provider of a service in a region faces no meaningful substitutes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some monopolists charge prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'Northgate is a monopolist' to 'Northgate charges above competitive prices.' Forcing that inference requires every monopolist to charge above competitive prices. (A) supplies the universal link.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. This guarantees only that above-competitive firms are monopolists, not that Northgate prices above the competitive level.
explanations.C: 'Tend to' falls short of certainty. Sufficient assumptions demand all, not a tendency.
explanations.D: Explains why Northgate counts as a monopolist but says nothing about its pricing.
explanations.E: 'Some' leaves open that Northgate belongs to the monopolists who do not price above competitive levels.

difficultyReason: One-step gap between 'contract signed under duress' and 'unenforceable.' The correct answer is the universal principle linking duress to unenforceability.
stimulus: Attorney: The settlement agreement that Rollins signed was obtained under duress, for the opposing party threatened to publicize confidential medical records unless he signed. It follows that the settlement agreement cannot be enforced against Rollins.
questionStem: The attorney's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No contract signed under duress can be enforced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any threat to publicize medical records constitutes duress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some contracts signed under duress cannot be enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any contract that cannot be enforced was signed under duress.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rollins signed the settlement agreement only because of the threat.

explanations.correct: The premise places the contract in the category 'signed under duress,' and the conclusion places it in 'cannot be enforced.' A universal from the first category to the second forces the conclusion. (A) does that.
explanations.B: Supports that what happened counts as duress, but duress is already granted in the premise.
explanations.C: 'Some' leaves open that Rollins's contract is one of the enforceable duress-signed contracts.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional. The argument needs duress → unenforceable, not the reverse.
explanations.E: Fills in a causal detail but does not connect duress to unenforceability, which is the unbridged step.

difficultyReason: Transparent one-step gap. Premise: the wetland is classified as an old-growth fen. Conclusion: it merits protection under the statute. The missing universal is the bridge.
stimulus: Ecologist: The Alderbrook wetland has been formally classified as an old-growth fen by the state survey. Therefore, the Alderbrook wetland merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act.
questionStem: The ecologist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every old-growth fen merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every wetland that merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act is an old-growth fen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most old-growth fens in the state have been formally classified by the state survey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No wetland can be classified as an old-growth fen unless it merits protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Wetlands Heritage Act protects wetlands that are rare or ecologically significant.

explanations.correct: The argument places Alderbrook in 'old-growth fen' and concludes it is in 'merits protection.' The universal 'every old-growth fen merits protection' is the missing link. (A) states precisely that.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: meriting protection → old-growth fen. Does not put Alderbrook into the protected category.
explanations.C: Shifts the subject to classification practice; irrelevant to whether Alderbrook merits protection.
explanations.D: This would be a requirement for classification, not an entailment from classification to protection.
explanations.E: Too vague — 'rare or ecologically significant' is not stipulated of Alderbrook, and protection is not guaranteed by this general description.

difficultyReason: Single transparent gap. Premise: the device uses end-to-end encryption. Conclusion: intercepted messages cannot be read by third parties. The universal that links the two is the needed assumption.
stimulus: The new Larkspur messaging app uses end-to-end encryption for all communications between users. It follows that any message sent through Larkspur cannot be read by a third party who intercepts it in transit.
questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No message protected by end-to-end encryption can be read by a third party who intercepts it in transit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any message that cannot be read by a third party who intercepts it is protected by end-to-end encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most messaging apps that use end-to-end encryption also encrypt stored copies of messages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: End-to-end encryption prevents third parties from determining who sent a given message.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Messages sent through Larkspur are encrypted on the sender's device before transmission.

explanations.correct: The argument classifies Larkspur messages as end-to-end encrypted and concludes they cannot be read by intercepting third parties. The universal in (A) forces that step.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: unreadable-if-intercepted → end-to-end encrypted. This does not place Larkspur messages in the unreadable category.
explanations.C: Shifts to stored copies; the conclusion concerns in-transit interception.
explanations.D: Introduces sender identity, a different property from message readability.
explanations.E: Provides a plausible mechanism but does not guarantee the interceptor cannot read the message.

difficultyReason: One-step gap between a linguistic property (derived from Proto-Indo-European) and a classification (Indo-European language). The universal bridge supplies the inference.
stimulus: Linguist: Tocharian B is a language whose vocabulary and grammar descend directly from Proto-Indo-European. It follows that Tocharian B is an Indo-European language.
questionStem: The linguist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any language whose vocabulary and grammar descend directly from Proto-Indo-European is an Indo-European language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every Indo-European language has a vocabulary and grammar that descend directly from Proto-Indo-European.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most languages classified as Indo-European are descended from Proto-Indo-European.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tocharian B shares vocabulary with several other Indo-European languages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No language is classified as Indo-European unless specialists agree on its ancestry.

explanations.correct: The premise places Tocharian B in the category 'descends from Proto-Indo-European.' The conclusion places it in 'Indo-European language.' (A) universalizes the move.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. It tells us a property of every Indo-European language, not that descent from PIE suffices for that classification.
explanations.C: 'Most' leaves room for Tocharian B to be an exception.
explanations.D: Shared vocabulary is evidence, but the argument already stipulates direct descent; what is missing is the link to the classification.
explanations.E: Introduces a gatekeeping condition about specialists that the stimulus never invokes.

difficultyReason: Direct one-step gap. Premise: the document was issued by the royal chancery before 1154. Conclusion: it must be written in Medieval Latin. The universal from category A to category B is the needed assumption.
stimulus: Historian: The charter granting market rights to the village of Ashworth was issued by the royal chancery during the reign of Henry I, which ended in 1154. It follows that the original text of the charter was written in Medieval Latin.
questionStem: The historian's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every document issued by the royal chancery before 1154 was written in Medieval Latin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any document written in Medieval Latin was issued by the royal chancery before 1154.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most surviving charters from the reign of Henry I are written in Medieval Latin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medieval Latin was used throughout Western Europe for official documents during the twelfth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The charter granting market rights to Ashworth has been preserved in its original form.

explanations.correct: The argument places the charter in the class 'issued by the royal chancery before 1154' and concludes it is in 'written in Medieval Latin.' The universal in (A) forces that move.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. It tells us the provenance of every Medieval Latin document, not the language of every pre-1154 chancery document.
explanations.C: 'Most' allows the charter to be among the exceptions.
explanations.D: Even if broadly true, it does not establish that this particular charter was in Medieval Latin rather than, say, Old English or Old French.
explanations.E: Preservation status is irrelevant to the original language.

difficultyReason: Single-step gap between 'raises effective tax rates on low-income households' and 'should be rejected by the council.' The universal principle linking the two closes the gap directly.
stimulus: Policy analyst: The proposed sales-tax expansion would raise the effective tax rate on low-income households in our district. Therefore, the council should reject the proposal.
questionStem: The analyst's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The council should reject any proposal that would raise the effective tax rate on low-income households.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any proposal the council rejects would have raised the effective tax rate on low-income households.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most proposals that raise taxes on low-income households also fail to raise significant revenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The council has previously rejected tax proposals that burdened low-income households.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sales-tax expansions generally burden low-income households more than high-income households.

explanations.correct: The premise places the proposal in 'raises rates on low-income households.' The conclusion places it in 'should be rejected.' (A) is the universal that forces the jump.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: rejected → raises rates on low-income. Does not support the council's duty to reject this one.
explanations.C: Introduces revenue, a concern the argument never raised, and uses 'most,' which is too weak.
explanations.D: Past practice does not entail what the council should do now.
explanations.E: Supports the premise's plausibility rather than bridging premise to conclusion.

difficultyReason: One-step conditional gap. Premise: the painting was produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti. Conclusion: it employs tenebrist lighting. The universal bridging movement to technique is the needed assumption.
stimulus: Art historian: The oil painting recently acquired by the Kessel Museum was produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti during the 1620s. It follows that the painting employs tenebrist lighting.
questionStem: The art historian's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every painting produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti employs tenebrist lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every painting that employs tenebrist lighting was produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most 1620s paintings acquired by major museums employ tenebrist lighting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paintings that employ tenebrist lighting are typically more valuable than those that do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Utrecht Caravaggisti were influenced by the Italian painter Caravaggio.

explanations.correct: The premise places the painting in the class 'produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti'; the conclusion places it in 'employs tenebrist lighting.' The universal in (A) closes that gap.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. It says tenebrist paintings are all Utrecht Caravaggisti works, not that every Utrecht Caravaggisti work is tenebrist.
explanations.C: 'Most' leaves the possibility that this painting is one that does not employ tenebrism.
explanations.D: Market value has no bearing on the technique used.
explanations.E: Explains influence but does not entail that every Utrecht Caravaggisti painting is tenebrist.
